delano-american-legion.html:
The Delano American Legion Post #377 was organized in the spring of 1920.  There were forty-one charter members. The first officers of the post were Frank Brunkow, Commander; J. W. Lohmiller, Vice-Commander; Albert McEachern, Post Adjutant; Ury Hanseman, Post Finance Officer; and John Tomnitz, Post Historian.  Following a membership drive later that year, membership increased to sixty-one.
   The purpose of the organization and the reason every ex-serviceman should become a member as stated in 1920 were:
   1. Because a loyal American citizen, a veteran of the World War, should earnestly desire to help his country in peace, as well as in war.
   2. Being more fortunate than others who have served the United States during the World War, they should desire to help the sick, wounded, disabled and destitute veteran.
   3. The comradeship of mutual service forms a band between individuals who served in the World War that cannot be ignored.
   4. An organized American Legion is a strong factor is securing the United States against war.
   5. To promote and foster patriotism.
   6. There is a personal satisfaction in accomplishing good, and there is a feeling of pride in wearing the emblem of an organization that is universally recognized as a power for good in all communities.
   7. No class – no rank – just comrades.

The current Mission Statement, 100 years later, in 1921:
FOR GOD AND COUNTRY WE ASSOCIATE OURSELVES TOGETHER
FOR THE FOLLOWING PURPOSES:
   To uphold and defend the Constitution of the United States of America;
   To maintain law and order;
   To foster and perpetuate a one hundred percent Americanism;
   To preserve the memories and incidents of our associations in the Great Wars;
   To inculcate a sense of individual obligation to the community, state and nation;
   To combat the autocracy of both the classes and the masses;
   To make right the master of might;
   To promote peace and goodwill on earth;
   To safeguard and transmit to posterity the principles of justice, freedom and democracy;
   To consecrate and sanctify our comradeship by our devotion to mutual helpfulness.

The Delano Legion is active in many community affairs.  They sponsor Legion Baseball and Boys State candidates. They have taken charge of the Memorial Day and Veterans Day programs. The Legion provides the Color Guard that leads the 4th of July Parade, and military honors at the funeral of veterans.  They continue to be an active community organization.

A memorial for the American Legion was erected in 2021 as part of an Eagle Scout project by Dillon Field.  Leading up to the monument is a path of engraved bricks honoring both active and deceased military and auxiliary members.  The monument reads:

For God and Country We Associate Ourselves Together for the Following Purposes
       To uphold and defend the Constitution of the United States of America;
       To maintain law and order;
       To foster and perpetuate a one hundred percent Americanism;
       To preserve the memories and incidents of our association in the Great Wars;
       To inculcate a sense of individual obligation to the community, state and nation;
       To combat the autocracy of both the classes and the masses;
       To make right the master of might;
       To promote peace and goodwill on earth;
       To safeguard and transmit to posterity the principles of justice, freedom and  democracy;
       To consecrate and sanctify our comradeship by our devotion to mutual helpfulness.

One of the bricks in this memorial commemorates Sgt. Dillon J, Semolina, a 2010 graduate of Delano High School.

Sgt. Semolina was killed in a nighttime training accident in 2016 when two Sikorsky CH-53E Super Stallion helicopters collided over the Pacific Ocean off Oahu’s North Shore in Hawaii.  Twelve marines, all of the crew members of both helicopters, were killed in the accident.     

Sgt. Dillon Semolina’s body was never recovered.

delano-creamery.html: The Delano Creamery began in 1895 when local banker C. G. Roosen, hoping to improve difficult economic conditions for area farmers, established a creamery after an initial attempt to organize a cooperative drew little support. Through persistent efforts to recruit farmers and arrange milk-hauling routes, the business quickly grew, and in 1898 local farmers purchased the operation and formed the Delano Co-operative Creamery Association. By 1909, the creamery had become one of the area’s leading manufacturing and shipping industries, with much of its product shipped to New York City, and its award-winning butter earned Delano a reputation for quality. By 1915 it served about 220 patrons and received milk from an estimated 1,800 cows, while buttermaker Emil G. Oman was recognized as a national champion. The operation later shifted largely to bottling milk and cream for local and Minneapolis markets. The creamery closed in the 1970s, and after housing other businesses for a time, the building was demolished in 2006; Delano’s sculpture walk now occupies the former site.

Located on River Street South

Line drawing for the Eagle’s Special Holiday Edition, 1898.

The following excerpt is from a letter to the Delano Eagle, published January 6, 1921, in a special section of Reminiscences of Delano, written by C. G. Roosen, talking about how he started the creamery in Delano:

“But I had real pleasure with the start of the Creamery in the spring of 1895. Those were hard times for everybody, especially for the farmers. Hogs, live weight, 2 ½ cents, rye 20 cents, wheat 50 cents and up, homemade butter 8 cents in trade; except to a few who had regular customers in Minneapolis the year found. I had been told that in the southern part of the state co-operative farmers’ creameries had been very successful and given universal satisfaction. I talked this matter over with Professor Haecker of the Agricultural college, and he advised me to arrange a meeting of the farmers at Delano. This meeting was attended by about one hundred farmers and was addressed by myself and Prof. Haecker. I had several subscription lists prepared which I handed to farmers residing in different directions from Delano and I asked them to interview their neighbors and have those who would be willing to take shares of $50.00 each in a co-operative creamery sign their names. I called a meeting in one week to get reports and take further steps. At the end of the week I had only three shares signed for.

I was much disappointed for I knew there were cows enough in the surrounding country to make the creamery a success if properly handled and I hated to let the matter fail and decided to investigate further, and if I felt encouraged to do so, start the creamery myself.

So I visited Owatonna, Albert Lea, and smaller towns near there. Everybody I talked with, hotel men, storekeepers, drivers and farmers, said “creameries are the best thing in the country.” Then the only thing to do was to decide on the size of the building, where and what machinery to buy, and take on an efficient buttermaker.

Mr. Swan Erickson built the creamery, Fargo and Co. furnished the machinery, and Mr. Chas. Kaemmerse became the efficient and popular buttermaker.

The opening of the creamery took place in early June, when everybody had plenty of milk and we received enough milk in June, July, and August to do a fair business for the one separator.

After that the few patrons I had had little milk left and the business seemed to run the course predicted by many of the larger farmers when they told me “Friend Roosen, now you are going into a business you know nothing about. You will never get my milk. I have too good an outlet the year round at 20 or 25 cents a pound in Minneapolis.” I could name a half dozen well-known and prominent farmers who spoke like that at that time. One year later, however, I heard from none of these “I told you so.”

Coming back to August 1895, the milk receipts were next to nothing and even my good friend Edwin Kelsey told me “I guess you will have to close the creamery for the winter.” It was up to me to get busy. I visited farm after farm trying to get the farmers to undertake joint hauling of milk to the creamery but I was generally met with the reply “let my neighbors come and see me about this.” I had to get a start in another way. I hired, I think, three farmers’ teams of different directions and paid them $45.00 a month to make daily trips to the creamery and pick up milk cans on their routes. Then I took my buggy loaded with new milk cans, many afternoons, and visited the good farmers wives and asked them to try and send the milk one month on trial. I left a milk can which cost $1.75 and agreed to take it back if after one month’s trial they did not want to send milk any longer. I do not remember ever getting one of those cans back.

When December came I received so much milk that I had to install a second De Laval separator. The price I paid the farmers for the month of December, 21 cents per pound of butter fat, was quite satisfactory at that time and I was enabled to obtain a better profit on the investment than I had figured on.

After three years the farmers naturally desired to own the creamery to which they faithfully hauled the milk and I did the best for everybody, myself included, and sold out my interest to them.”

(from The Delano Eagle, September 19, 1907)

“The new creamery building is now completed and the board of directors will have a meeting this week to settle with the contractors. Secretary Ziebarth is planning arrangements for a big meeting of the stockholders, patrons and farmers generally, to be held soon, when able speakers from the University will be present and deliver addresses. It is Mr. Ziebarth’s intention to increase patronage of the creamery to a great number as the capacity of the concern is now such that it will be able to handle nearly double what it has been doing.”

(from The Great Northwestern Magazine, Wright County Edition, December 1909)

“Since the advent of the Delano Creamery Association ten years ago, the business has made rapid strides, until now the concern ranks among the leading manufacturing and shipping industries in this section of Minnesota. During this time the company has gained a reputation for itself as a loyal booster for Delano in fact, the association claims the unique distinction of being the originators of the phrase “Boost for the best town in the county.” The company started on a small scale, at first simply handling the milk of a few farmers, but with its rapid growth new improvements have been added, and this summer completed a new building 36x46 and an addition 30x40, at a cost of $7,000, thus affording the association a home second to none in the state of Minnesota. The plant, buildings and holdings have grown from a small concern to an industry with buildings and equipment worth in the neighborhood of $12,000. Their product is shipped for the most part to New York City, where it sells always at top notch figures, thus insuring its hundreds of staunch farmer friends the most money obtainable for their milk and cream. Mr. Mat Schaust is the president, ably assisted by Wm. Ziebarth in the capacity of secretary and manager. The mere statement of the fact that Mr. Ziebarth has to do with the business end of this company gives assurance of success. Its members were fortunate in securing his services in so important a position. Mr. Ziebarth has been honored time and again by the voters of Delano and Wright County in his selection to offices of importance and trust, not the least of which was his election as a member of the board of county commissioners. He is also vice-president of the State Bank of Delano and stands high in the estimation of all its people.

(from The History of Wright County, Vol. II, 1915):

“C.G. Roosen, then a resident banker of Delano, built and equipped a plant and commenced operating in the spring of 1895. December 20, 1897, the Delano Co-operative Creamery Association was organized by Edwin Kelsey, Louis Bock, Carl Schroeder, Christian Buch, Joseph Muckenhirn, Joseph Kelsey, Louis Kespohl, John Matter and Math. Schaust. February 1, 1898, this association purchased the building and entire equipment of Mr. Roosen, and took immediate possession, employing Charles Kramer as buttermaker and Nels Sandberg as helper. This was the beginning of what is today a prosperous farmers’ co-operative institution, owned and managed by farmers. In 1907 the old structure was replaced by a large and well-equipped brick building. The old-fashioned creamery appliances have been replaced by new and modern machinery, and now ranks will among the most up-to-date creameries in the state. The present buttermaker is Emil G. Oman, whose make of butter is of the finest quality and scores exceptionally high in scoring contests, proving him to be a buttermaker of exceptional ability. At the convention of the National Creamery Buttermakers’ Association, held in Mason City, Iowa, in March 1915, he was declared to be the champion buttermaker of the country by the committee of awards. The creamery has an average of 220 patrons and receives the product from (estimated) 1,800 cows. The cows are mostly of common stock, with here and there, however, a Guernsey and a Holstein.”
The Delano Co-operative Creamery became widely known almost immediately for the fine quality of its products. Delano creamery butter won several prizes, including one at the Buffalo World’s Fair.
The creamery closed in the 1970’s and the building became the home to other businesses until it was torn down in 2006.

By 1946 the creamery’s activities were almost entirely devoted to bottling milk and cream for local as well as Minneapolis consumption. The creamery employed eleven men at that time and was managed by Herbert Bauman.

delano-municipal-utilities.html: Delano’s municipal utilities grew alongside the community, beginning with streetlights and a city well in 1879 and expanding after voters approved bonds for electric lights and waterworks in 1894. The original power plant on South River Street used a wood-burning steam engine, while wells and a water tower supplied water for both fire protection and household use. As demand increased, Delano expanded electric service, established 24-hour A.C. service in 1915, built its own distribution system in 1927, and opened a new diesel power plant in 1932—making Delano the only town in Wright County with a municipally owned light and power plant. The system continued to modernize with larger generators, expanded facilities, a new substation, a major water tower in 2002, and a new water treatment plant in 2006. The utility also weathered some of Delano’s most dramatic floods, including the 1965 flood, when a Navy helicopter rescued five men stranded inside the flooded power plant because the Crow River was too dangerous for a boat rescue.

The village of Crow River was platted in 1868. The name was changed to Delano in 1870, and the town was incorporated in 1876. As the town grew, so did its need for municipal improvements.  Ten streetlights were installed in 1879 “at the most necessary points on our streets” and a city well dug.  By 1893 the local citizens were indicating that the town should have electric lights and a system of waterworks. A petition was presented to the city council asking that the council call a special election for considering the matters of establishing waterworks and of putting in a four and a half foot dam. A special election was held in April 1894 to consider the proposition of issuing ten $1,000 bonds for waterworks and electric lights. It passed with 128 in favor and 64 votes against.

The building was erected on south River Street, on the east bank of the Crow River and about on block north of what is now Highway 12. The power plant was a direct current distribution system with wood-burning steam engine generating equipment. It was decided to use the water system not only for fire protection, but also for domestic use. Thus, they abandoned the idea of using the river as a water source, and put in wells and a water tower. When the waterworks were completed an agreement was made with the Great Northern Railway Co. to furnish that company with water for its water tanks at Delano.

In the early years electricity was available only in the evening hours, but in 1898 it was also made available for use in the morning. People on the west side of town wanted electricity out past the west end of the bridge and up the Watertown road.  In April of 1907 the council decided to use coal instead of wood as fuel at the powerhouse and also to shut off the water at night. In December of that same year it was decided to extend the electric lights to the west side of the river.

By 1915 D.C. current was not considered ample and the power plant was not efficient. Local citizens convinced the then Minneapolis General Electric Co. to build an A.C. current high line, and 24 hour electric service was established.  In 1927 Delano built its own electric distribution system.  Delano was the only town in Wright County to have a municipally owned light and power plant. With its population expanding, once again capacity was being reached. An election was held in 1931 to vote on the issue of building a new diesel power plant. The vote was 437 yes and 36 no. The new building was erected on the west end of the bridge over the Crow River, on a site that for many years had been lumber yards, and opened for use on January 12, 1932.
The power plant and the transformer station were surrounded by sandbags during the 1957 flood.

Again the power plant flooded during the 1965 flood, and a Navy helicopter was necessary to rescue five men stranded in the facility: Leonard Logston, Milton Voltin, Darwin Voltin, George Schaar and Edward Libor. The waters were too high and the current too fast for boat rescue.

Delano is a member of the Central Minnesota Municipal Power Agency, which is compromised of 16 members municipalities located in the State of Minnesota, each of which owns and operates an electric generation and distribution system.  It is through the association with the Agency that the Delano Municipal Utility is able to negotiate long-term low cost wholesale power.

hildebrandt-bldg.html: The Rockford Woolen Mills Co. to Riverside Commons

The Rockford Woolen Mills Co. – to – Riverside Commons

(from The Minneapolis Journal, Tuesday, November 7, 1905)

MILLS TO BE MOVED

Delano Organizes Company to Secure Rockford Industry

DELANO, MINN. – A company has been organized here with a capital stock of $15,000, of which $10,000 is already paid up, for the purpose of moving the machinery of the Rockford Woolen mills to this place. The following officers have been selected: George P. Schaffer, president; J. E. Borsch, vice president; Charles E. Parker, secretary; L.P. Probst, treasurer, The board of directors are: J. E. Borsch, Adam Horsch, A. L. Mealey, M.E. Muckey, E. T. Ziebarth, F. J. Benner and Frank Roban.

A site will be selected and the erection of a building commenced at once. The woolen mill will give employment to many, and will make quite an addition to the business of interested of Delano. Should the business of the concern warrant, the mills will be increased to double its present capacity and more stock to cover the expense of building will be sold. This can be easily done, as the $10,000 in shares were sold in less than one day’s work, and many other citizens were still anxious to buy.”

(from The Delano Eagle, November 16, 1905)

“The site of the woolen mills has been selected – part of the Ed Bock property on the west side. The piece was purchased for a consideration of $1,000. Work on the foundation of the building will be commenced at once and the structure erected as fast as possible so as to get the machinery in place in a few months. Mr. Brenner is anxious to begin work on his next year’s orders and every effort will be made to push the work forward.”

(from the Delano Eagle, November 23, 1905)

“The foundation for the woolen mills is about completed and the work of erecting the building will be commenced at once. The ground around the site is being graded and put in good shape to allow easy access to the building with teams. The way this enterprise is being carried to completion speaks loud for the business push of those who have taken hold of the industry.”

(from The Delano Eagle, December 14, 1905)

“A large crew of men are at work on the woolen mill and rushing it rapidly forward. It will not be many days before another steam whistle will announce that the wheels of this industry have been set in motion.”

(from The Delano Eagle, January 11, 1906)

“F. J. Benner and family arrived last Thursday from points in Wisconsin where they had visited and are now occupying their rooms in the new brick block. Mr. Benner informs us that he will commence this week the work of placing the machinery in the new building, and the work will be pushed forward as rapidly as possible.”

(from The Delano Eagle, January 11, 1906)

“A meeting of the directors of the Woolen Mill Co. was held last Monday evening and one of the important matters for consideration was the purchasing of an engine, boiler and elevator. Mr. Reichard, representing a Minneapolis firm, was present explaining the qualities of his goods. Several price lists were submitted by different firms and after considerable discussion, Mr. Muckey and Mr. Horsch were appointed a committee to do the purchasing. They will go to the city this week to attend to the matter as the building is now ready for the placing of this part of the equipment.”

(from The Delano Eagle, March 22, 1906)

AN UP-TO-DATE FACTORY

___________

The Rockford Mills Company is Adding New Machinery and Fitting Up Its Plant in First-Class Shape

“In order to be thoroughly up-to-date, the Rockford Woolen Mills Company has purchased several new pieces of machinery which are expected to arrive at any time and which will make their mill one of the most complete in the country. It is the policy of the directors to expend sufficient money to get rid of any handicap that might stand in the way of producing goods at the least possible cost. More money has been expended upon the equipment than was at first thought necessary, but every dollar has been spent with a view to obtaining the best results when operations are commenced. Anybody visiting the mill will readily see that the equipment is first-class in every way and that a permanent and prosperous industry is planned. The market for such goods as the mill will turn out is practically unlimited and the margins of profit are very satisfactory. All that is necessary is to keep the quality of the goods up and to work the factory to its full capacity all the year round, and this can easily be done through the system of steam heating that has been installed.

In order to furnish ample working capital and to take advantage of discounts, etc., the directors have decoded to dispose of the remainder of the stock which will no doubt, be readily taken up by local parties. The business integrity and standing of those interested insures an honest and efficient management and the investment will no doubt prove a very profitable and satisfactory one.”

(from The Delano Eagle, 19__ _)

At the meeting of the stockholders of the woolen mill a bid from the Lundsten Lumber Co. was received in which $3,000 was offered for the concern. By a vote of the stock the bid was accepted but when the impression was allowed to prevail that the company intended tearing the building down and disposing of the machinery a strenuous kick was registered, which was so strong that the bid was withdrawn. This leaves the woolen mill situation as it has been for the past year. There seems to be no solution to the difficulty in the way o getting the mill running again. What the outcome will be is hard to say. The slight indebtedness is liable to eat up all the money invested unless some disposition can be made of the property whereby it will be operated. Should this prove to be the case it is liable to injure any industry which might be brought up for consideration in the future The greatest difficulty seems to lie in the fact that for the past few years like institutions have suffered a loss because of a plethora of woolen goods on the market, which has forced prices down so that the goods cannot be manufactured at a profit and the capital invested has had no return whatever. Another hindrance is that goods have to be sold nearly a year in advance and in this it would be necessary to have a man on the road at a fair salary in order to know just how much would have to be turned out. This of course takes more capital than the stockholders care to put up. But such things have got to be considered in cases of this kind.”

(from the Delano Eagle,19__ )

“M. E. Muckey and Oscar Hildebrandt have purchased the woolen mill for a consideration of $12.00 per share, they assuming all the indebtedness, the total consideration being about $3,200. Muckey & Hildebrandt will open a repair shop and automobile garage for the present and will no doubt do a good business, as both are expert mechanics. Later on they intend to add other enterprises to their shop, one of which we hear reported as being a steam laundry. They will dispose of he machinery used in the woolen mill, which will give them ample space for all kinds of work.”

(from The Delano Eagle, Milton E Muckey obituary, January 24, 1937)

“When Delano business men took over the Rockford woolen mill and moved it to Delano, he installed most of the machinery. Later on he and O. B. Hildebrandt purchased the woolen mill property and started an automobile garage which was the first Ford agency in Wright County. In 1922, Mr. Muckey retired and the agency was transferred to Mr. Hildebrandt, who now handles Chevrolet motor cars and trucks.”

(from The Delano Eagle, Oscar Hildebrandt obituary)

“He (Oscar Hildebrandt) went into the automobile business with his brother-in-law, Milton Muckey in 1912. He and Mr. Muckey had one of the first automobile agencies in the county. Mr. Hildebrandt was in the automobile business in Delano until 1939.”

1912 photo - Milton Muckey and Oscar Hildebrandt were the owners of the Delano Auto Company, the first Ford agency in Wright County. They were located in the former Rockford Woolen Mills building site, across from the current Power Plant. When Mr. Muckey retired, Mr. Hildebrandt switched to Chevrolets. Later, this became Bostrom Chevrolet, Zwick Chevrolet, Walsh Chevrolet, Western Gas and now the Riverside Commons building.

Harry R. Zwick, owner of Zwick Motor Company left the 260 acre farm along with his brother, G. E. Zwick, now of Minneapolis in 1913 and moved to Lake City where they entered the automobile business. Seeing a need for automobiles among farmers the Zwick brothers were the very first to own a gasoline tractor in 1908. Folks in the vicinity laughed at the brothers and it was quite a novelty in those days, but they were able to finish their threshing that year, long before the neighbors.

After eight years in business there, the brothers dissolved the partnership n 1923 and Mr. Zwick moved to Red Wing where he took an automobile agency. Ill health in 1929 forced him to sell out and retire from business for a few years. In 1935 he again took over an automobile agency at Rochester where he continued until he sold out during March 1939. He then came to Delano where he opened his location during June of the same year. He has been the Chevrolet dealer here since.

(from the Mainstreet, a special edition of The Delano Eagle, 1946)
Walsh Chevrolet, surrounded by the April 1965 flood waters.

indigenous-people.html: Long before Delano was founded, the land along the Crow River was part of the homeland of the Dakota people, who had lived in relationship with the land for centuries. Their presence remains reflected in many Minnesota place names, including Minnesota itself, derived from the Dakota Mni Sota, meaning “cloudy water” or “sky-tinted water.” The Dakota moved seasonally between winter camps in protected woodlands and summer homes near water and planting grounds, hunting, gathering, gardening, and passing their history and traditions from one generation to the next. Central to Dakota life was an understanding that people were related to the earth, water, plants, animals, and sky and therefore had a responsibility to care for them. This land was not simply a place the Dakota passed through—it was their home. Delano’s later settlement and development took place only after Dakota people had been displaced from their homeland through treaties, forced removal, violence, and exile, making their history an essential first chapter in understanding the story of Delano.

The story of Delano begins with the story of the land on which the city was founded. Delano’s beginning was possible only because Dakota people, who for centuries had lived on and identified the land as their relative, had been pushed to reservations, killed, or exiled out of Minnesota. Evidence of their presence is in the very names of places throughout the state, including Minnetonka, Chaska, Cokato, Wayzata, and Minnesota.

“When the first white men penetrated this area in the seventeenth century, most of the area was held by the Dakota. The Dakota, having been here for hundreds of years, had named all the landmarks. The name Minnesota is a Dakota word, Mni sota, which means “cloudy water” or “sky-tinted water.” The name became official at its statehood in 1858. 

As the seasons changed, the Dakota moved making their rounds upon the land, repeating the pattern year after year. Summers were hot and winters were very cold. 

With the arrival of winter, the Dakota moved to the protection of the woods to set up tepees. They pegged the walls (mostly made from deer skins) to the ground and piled snow around the edges to keep out the wind. They gathered around the fires built in the center of the tepees. This was the time that the older Dakota men taught the next generation and their children about the history of their people and the ways of the Dakota through story-telling, reciting the well-known stories over and over. They told their children how they believed they were related to all things: the earth, the trees, the sky, the sun and all animals. Everything in creation needed to be respected and treated as it was a relative of theirs. ‘Our people lived not just on the land but with the land, and felt a responsibility to it, to care for it, because it cared for us,’ states Gwen Westerman in an interview conducted by Gwen Briesemeister for the Delano Oral History Sesquicentennial Project (2025).
Seth Eastman paintings – Indian Sugar Camp and Dakota Encampment

The women and children along with the older men, collected fallen branches for firewood. The young men were tasked with using bows and arrows to hunt for food which included deer, moose, elk and sometimes bison. These tribal customs and routines were practiced year after year, for centuries. Everyone played a role in the survival of the Dakota family. The flow of life for them was like a song.

In the late spring, the Dakota gathered at their summer places, close to where they would plant their gardens. Thus, they chose areas of soft, sandy ground close to water. Here they built large semi-permanent houses made from poles and bark and returned to these structures year after year. The Dakota moved as the weather dictated. This movement may have been interpreted as ‘just passing through,’ but the changing of homesites was the Dakota way, differing from how modern-day Americans define home. To them all of the land, including hunting grounds, was their home.’

from Marcia Brakke’s book, Delano on the Crow: 150 Years of Unrivaled Spirit

There are numerous resources to learn more about the Dakota people. Two of the best are Hoċokata Ṫi Cultural Center in Shakopee and the Minnesota Historical Society in St. Paul. Below is a remarkable interactive video that focuses on “westward expansion” and the treaties made (and broken) with Dakota people.

leiter-oil-company.html: Founded in 1912 by Frank and Oscar Leiter, the Leiter Oil Company became a longtime fixture of Delano’s automotive history and held the distinction of being the oldest independent jobber with Pure Oil. The Leiter filling station at Bridge Avenue and Highway 12 was built in 1923, and Oscar Leiter went on to operate the oil company while also becoming a prominent local automobile dealer. The business weathered repeated Crow River floods, including major flooding in 1952, 1957, and 1965, before Oscar’s son Edward sold the company in 1969. Over the years, changes in ownership and oil companies transformed the service station into Adolph’s Union 76, while the Leiter Auto Company evolved into a Ford dealership. The Leiter automotive legacy remains visible in Delano today: Absolute Automotive and Brinkman’s Trailers.

The Leiter Oil Company was started in 1912 by Frank and Oscar Leiter, who signed with the Pure Oil Company. Leiter’s had the proud distinction of being the oldest independent jobber with Pure Oil.

Oscar Leiter was born in 1898 in Woodland township. He began working in his father’s (Frank Leiter) automobile garage when still in his teens and became a long-time prominent businessman in Delano, eventually taking over the Leiter Oil Company as well as becoming a Buick and Pontiac dealer.

The filling station on the corner of Bridge Avenue and Highway 12 (then Highway 10), was built in 1923, the “finishing touches” being applied in July.
It was plastered outside and covered with crushed marble, giving it a wonderfully ornamental exterior, according to the Delano Eagle.

(from the Mainstreet, a special edition of the Eagle, 1946) – The Super Service Station on Highway 12.

“Oscar Leiter, owner of the Leiter Oil Company, has been in business here for the past 25 years.. Quality products plus courteous service have helped to make this one of Delano’s most popular service stations.”
Oscar Leiter, Carol Leiter, and Juanita Kaiser, ca. 1940

The service station greatly suffered during the flooding of the Crow River. In 1952, possibly the greatest individual loss, as reported in the Delano Eagle, was suffered by Oscar Leiter whose home, apartment building and two rental houses as well as filling station and garage were flooded.
Leiter’s Pure Oil station in the 1952 flood.

plotniks-blacksmith.html: For more than a century, Plotnik’s Blacksmith Shop stood as a reminder of the craftsmanship, ingenuity, and work ethic that helped build the Delano community. Founded in 1887 by Polish immigrant and blacksmith Paul Plotnik, the business grew from a small rented shop into a thriving operation producing and repairing the wagons, farm implements, tools, and equipment needed by a growing agricultural community. Paul’s son Louis joined the business, and later generations adapted the shop as horses gave way to tractors and modern machinery, creating everything from flagpoles and church crosses to custom metalwork. Although the forge eventually quieted, the Plotnik family’s long tradition of blacksmithing and community service remains an important link to Delano’s early history and the skilled trades that helped shape the town.

In the corridors of humanity, on the paths of ingenuity and imagination, legends are made. Some are heroic and dramatic; some are minor and modest. Legends are stories of human growth, the evolution of mind and matter, and the records of people. Undimmed and undarkened, both prominent and modest, Plotnik’s Blacksmith Shop is a local legend. It stands on Highway 12 as a testimony to the work ethic and civic values that helped establish the Delano community on the South Fork of the Crow River.

The city of Delano was founded in 1868 and incorporated in 1876. In 1887, a Polish immigrant, Paul Plotnik, born on January 15, 1869, immigrated from his home in the Oppeln, upper Silesia, Poland. He was a locksmith by trade and came to America seeking new ideas, skills and opportunities. Before settling in Delano, Plotnik lived in other Minnesota communities and honed his skills as a blacksmith and farrier. He opened his first shop in 1889, renting a small building on the corner of River Street and Elm Avenue. As the city grew and agriculture became diverse, there was need for multiple tools, implements, devices, and gadgets to meet the demands of mid-century America’s expansion in industry, agriculture and commerce. Plotnik built a larger shop in 1891 on the other side of River Street, the area later occupied by Delano Granite Works display area.

Louis Plotnik, Paul’s younger brother, worked for him as a blacksmsith.

Plotnik continued to expand his business, eventually adding two warehouses in addition to the main building.

(from The Great Northwest Magazine, December 1909)

PAUL PLOTNIK - A city which receives the amount of grain first hand that Delano does must of necessity and naturally have a very large trade in agricultural implements and machinery. Mr. Paul Plotnik has an establishment containing a full line of farm machinery, buggies, wagons, bob sleighs, hayracks, wagon boxes and spring seats. This immense stock is housed in a building 24x40, with an addition 10x40 and in connection are two warehouses, 36x50 and 16x36. Three competent men are employed in the manufacture of wagons, seats, bobs and hay racks, the last of which is widely known as Plotnik’s patent hay rack. Mr. Plotnik has been engaged in business here for eighteen years. To have an inventor, who through careful thought and investigation of means and ways has been able to give to the community a product so complete in its mechanism, so substantial in its structure, is an honor few cities can boast of. Mr. Plotnik also conducts a first class blacksmith and horse shoeing shop and in this line has the liberal support of all Wright county farmers.”
In this 1910 advertisement from the Delano Eagle, Plotnik advertised his new building, “Up-to-Date” buggies, surreys, carriages, top buggies, platform wagons, and farm wagons.

Paul built a new shop on Highway 12 in 1933. The new facility represented Plotnik’s transition from the agricultural period when horse-drawn equipment was locally constructed and repaired using traditional blacksmithing techniques such as the forge and anvil. In the early 20th century, Plotnik responded to changing agricultural practices by providing welding services and using belt-driven equipment. It was a thriving business. In 1945, after service in World War II, son, George, took over the family business. As the demand for blacksmithing services diminished, George branched out, fabricating flagpoles, swing sets, church projects, picnic tables. Examples of Plotnik’s craft dot the community, including the three original flag poles at the Delano City Hall.

A nineteenth century blacksmith shop bears little likeness to today’s technological/digital industries. The shop is a monument to a pioneering spirit that spanned three centuries, and brought agriculture, commerce, industry and services to area communities. Now in its third generation, the family name, in hand-crafted letters, stands out among the neon lights and automated messages that populate Highway 12. Grandsons Tim and Tom Plotnik continue to operate the blacksmith shop on a part-time basis. Tim constructed a flagpole by his parents’ head stone in St. Joseph’s cemetery.

Paul Plotnik contributed to the community by his support of retail growth. He was the inventor of the Plotnik patent hay rack. He was one of the organizers and helped build St. Joseph’s Church of which he was a member. Because he had the unusual skill of fluency in four languages, as a side line, Plotnik worked as an interpreter in the Wright County Court system. Locally, he was considered both a laborer and a linguist and was helpful as the population increased. Paul Plotnik was a charter member of the Delano fire department when it was formed 1896.

An early sign of the Plotnik’s influence in the community was his support for our country’s defense efforts. His son Charley served in World War I and was one of the first commanders of the Delano American Legion. After George returned from World War II, he took over the family business. One of George’s first projects was construction of a “Welcome Veterans” sign. The modest sign takes on significance as travelers on Highway 12 are reminded of our common history and feelings.
George was a member of the Delano American Legion.

Crafted by trained hands, engineered by imagination, livelihood, and necessity, Plotnik’s trademark was seen throughout the community and neighboring rural areas. The passing of time has not diminished the impact of strong hands, hard work, and skilled metallurgy. The old-fashioned images of a blacksmith as a specialist in the metal trades working mainly with iron and steel using a forge for soldering is a familiar local memory. The vivid images of hammering, pounding, smithing, and shaping tools and devices, swing sets, plowshares, pillars and gates, lattice and grills to furnish homes, farms, schools and businesses are an aspect of daily life in the community. The vast metal industry was essential to the progress of the country. It produced and continues to produce massive structures such as freeways and skyscrapers, industrial and commercial buildings, rocket ships, bridge decks, and military equipment and the countless columns, poles and pillars across the nation that support the heartbeat and the lifestyle of America and the Delano community.

Well into the future passersby on the highway will slow down, stop, glimpse, and feel. Altered only slightly by the weight of time, the Blacksmith shop pays homage to pioneer times, courageous people, hard work and metal and stone. If you visited the blacksmith shop today, you would see relics of industry and human effort. A tour of Delano today will discover and uncover many historic sites. Plotnik’s Blacksmith shop is an icon of people and progress, of art and architecture that withstands time. Much has changed. Much has remained the same. - Ted May
Paul Plotnik and his wife Elizabeth (nee Lyrek) were the parents of eleven children. Paul died in 1948.

rieder-homestead.html: The Rieder barn was built in 1881 by Andrew Rieder (1836-1911) who emigrated from Baudenbach, Bavaria, Germany in 1861.  It was part of the original homestead.
View from hill on the back of the homestead behind the barn.

The barn, which once housed cattle, chickens and pigeons in the pigeon house on the roof. Later, he used it as a woodworking and blacksmithing shop. His great-grandchildren, twins Dave and Dan Rieder, restored the barn in 1980 and used it for their own woodworking and neighborhood get-togethers.  Since 2016, the Rieder Homestead has been the site of “Rieder Homestead Concerts”, a nationally recognized private music series. .  In May 21, 2016 the first concert was performed in the Rieder Homestead Barn. It is now a venue for live music concerts.

There have been five generations on this homestead block of Bridge Ave, where the barn stands. Andrew, his nephew and son in law, Leonard (L.J.), who started the Rieder Meat Market, his son Laurence Rieder, and Laurence's children.  Both Leonard and Laurence Sr. were Delano City Mayors.

One of Andrew's wagons still at the Rieder Barn

Andre Rieder and August Sieloff built wagons and sleighs at their workshop on North River St.

the-drive-in.html: Since opening as an A&W Drive-In in 1957, Delano’s beloved drive-in at 115 Babcock Boulevard has been much more than a place for burgers, fries, and root beer—it has been a community gathering place where generations of young people worked, friends met, and lasting memories were made. After operating for years as the Delano Drive-In, Mike and Vickie Mirenda purchased the business in 1982 and eventually transformed it into the unmistakable pink Peppermint Twist, complete with its famous raspberry shakes and whimsical Teddy Bear Park. Remarkably, the original 1957 building remains, and the tradition continues through generations of employees—including daughters and granddaughters of some of the original carhops. Today, the Peppermint Twist remains a nostalgic Delano destination where people come not only to eat, but to play, visit, and remember summers gone by.
The A & W was the local hangout in the 60’s, and it’s still considered, now as the Peppermint Twist, “the best!”
It began as an A & W Drive-In.

The first ad for the A & W Drive-in in Delano appeared May 23, 1957. But by June 13, 1957, it was under new management, that of Henry Holmberg and his wife Ruth. Harold and Joyce Nelson were the next owners, managing the drive-in for over 25 years, first as an A & W, and after losing the franchise, as the Delano Drive-In.

Memories from the A & W…

“I started working at the A&W when I was 15. In just a few days I turned 16 so I was "legal". Henry Holmberg and his wife, Ruth owned the place at that time. I was fortunate enough to work the kitchen, the front, and car hop. It was a fun place to work. Judy Grengs, Marcia Brandenburg, Nola Enos, Mary Lou Logsdon, Janet Bauman, Jean Buch, Alice Askov were some of the people I worked with. It was a fun job because everybody seemed to hang out there at some time during the summer.”

“Yes, I carhopped along with others from Delano High School about 1958-1960. It was a fun job, but we worked very hard most of the time as it was such a busy popular place to eat and meet friends. “

“I worked for Harold and Ruth the summer of 1966 with a number of class of 1967 girls. We worked hard but it was a fun job too.”

“My aunt Kay met her husband at the A & W. She was a car hop and he was a cook.”

“I started working at the A & W the summer before my 8th grade year. Such a fun job. I cooked with Colleen Klaers for at least 2 summers. I worked there 5 summers total. Lots of other girls worked there too, including my sister Shelly Smith.”

“I worked for Harold Nelson at the A & W through high school and college, cooking with Terri Traen and others, approximately from 1975 -1981.”

“Someone came in alone and ordered a root beer float from their car on the “ordermatic” when the carhop took it out, I pushed a wiener down into the ice cream and turned on the order machine in the building. As he drank the float, I heard him say “What the??!!! Traen!!!” as the wiener rose out of the ice cream. Working there wasn’t work. It was fun and everyone there was a blast.”

“I worked at the A&W when Harold would go to the County Fair.”

“Pam Diem worked with me too!”

“I worked at the A & W from the spring of 1974 to the end of June of 1976. Harold and Penny Ditty taught me how to run the kitchen. I remember telling Harold Nelson in late June of ‘76 that I was quitting on July 1st so I could attend court reporting school in Minneapolis starting Monday, July 5th. He looked at me and said, “Jean, you’re making the biggest mistake of your life.” I guess I should have stayed flipping burgers and making french fries for $1.25 an hour for the rest of my life.”

“I worked there the summer of ninth grade. We had moved to Delano from Loretto.”

“I loved working summers at the A & W 1976-1979. Having friends stop by and hang out at those walk-up windows are good memories. And working shifts with Kim Kusha, Patty Ditty, and Mary Kay Metz – so fun! Our boss, Harold was an interesting personality”

“I worked there the summer of 1980. I was a cook.”

The flood waters in 1965 were so high that only the roof of the drive-in was above water.

In 1982 Mike and Vickie Mirenda bought the Delano Drive-in from Kathy and Dewayne Platzer. It needed some work. Plans to have Italian food were abandoned as the drive-in became busier and busier. When Hardees came to Delano in 1988, they decided the old colors from the A & W had to go, and they painted the exterior of their building pink, instantly becoming the signature color for the Peppermint Twist. It drew people’s attention, and got them stopping in.

The famous raspberry shake was created when a salesman suggested tossing his raspberries into a shake. For a brief time, there was a mini-golf course on the north end. The first painted decorations were balloons and clowns, but that soon changed to teddy bears. The addition of hula-hoops in the fenced area soon developed into Teddy Bear Park. Over the years the fenced playground full of toys, the wishing well filled with treasures, the picnic tables, and the jukebox music added to the draw of burgers, fries, and the popular shakes.

A Teddy Bear fence now defines the west boundary. The building, with some remodeling, is the original from 1957, but the canopy was replaced in 2000 following a partial collapse after heavy snow. The Peppermint Twist attracts people from all over to eat, play, and have fun. WCCO voted it the Best Drive-In Restaurant in Minnesota in 2016, and it was again recognized in the 2017 Mpls. St. Paul magazine Best of Summer issue.

One of things Vickie and Mike emphasis is how great their staff is. Many of the girls that work there have been daughters and granddaughters of the girls that worked as carhops in the 50’s and 60’s

A recent comment was “I remember going there when it first opened, and we make it a destination every time we come back to Delano.”
“The raspberry shake is an all-time favorite!”

sesquicentennial.html:
Delano was founded in 1876 along the banks of the Crow River. What started as a small river town has grown into the community you're standing in today, built by generations who showed up for each other.

In 2026, Delano celebrated 150 years the way this town does everything: together. The celebration kicked off with a "150 Ways to Celebrate" campaign, giving the town 150 reasons to get involved throughout the year.
A few of the 150 Ways to Celebrate…
A historic 2026 calendar, filled with old photos and milestone dates from Delano's past, was given out free to the community thanks to local sponsors.
On February 11th, Delano's actual birthday, signs along Highway 12 were changed for the day to read "Happy Birthday, Delano," and the community gathered at City Hall to celebrate.
At the Chamber of Commerce "I Love Delano Dinner," city council members reenacted the original signing of the Delano Corporation, bringing the town's founding moment back to life.

On June 13, the Delano Area Council for Arts and Culture’s Sculpture and Blues Fest gave Delano something permanent. A new sculpture, created by James and Ryan Pedersen, stands as the centerpiece: four pillars representing the Crow River, agriculture, industry, and the railroad, with the number 150 formed in the space between them. A mural by Leanna Wurzer weaves in photos of over 2,000 tiles decorated by the community, and a path of Heritage Bricks are dedicated with personal messages to families, businesses, and organizations that make up Delano.
Local author Marcia Brakke published Delano on the Crow: 150 Years of Unrivaled Spirit, launched at the book at an elegant evening at the Jerome in June.

As home of the largest Fourth of July celebration in Minnesota, our celebration was one to remember marking both the nation's 250th birthday and the Delano's 150th in the same year, complete with a Delano 150 float in the parade!
It all came together on October 3rd at the Delano 150 Years Jamboree, a full day of music, food, and celebration that closed with the whole town singing "Happy Birthday" together.
